newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem warlord folk hero reburied in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Moslem warlord folk hero reburied in Sarajevo.

text.p: A Moslem brigade commander who was a folk hero to some for helping defend besieged Sarajevo but a vicious warlord to others was reburied in a military cemetery on Saturday in a ceremony attended by thousands.

The remains of Musan Topalovic, better known as "Caco", had lain in an unmarked grave for three years after he was shot dead in a government crackdown on his paramilitary gang of racketeers terrorising the capital.

Caco was exhumed this week, placed in a rough wooden casket draped in a black shroud inscribed with gold Arabic script, and carried by a frenzied mob of men shouting "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) to Kovaci military cemetery.

His final resting place is in the heart of Sarajevo's mediaeval Ottoman quarter, former base of operations for the 10th Mountain Brigade which he commanded along a key strip of battlefront on hillsides looming overhead.

The gravesite memorial service, conducted by a dozen Islamic imams among a mass of crouching mourners with Bosnian and brigade flags waving, amounted to a partial rehabilitation of Caco because the government made no attempt to stop it.
But no government representatives were known to have attended the rite which began with a funeral in a 16th century mosque near the old front line once held down by Caco's men.
Speakers at the cemetery eulogised Caco as a war hero without whom Sarajevo would have fallen to Serb besiegers early in the 1992-95 conflict which killed 10,000 city residents.

They made no mention of his reign of terror over downtown Sarajevo in 1992-93 in which his brigade members turned to gangsterism when off-duty, engaging in robbery, extortion and black marketeering to profit from siege shortages.

"You came home from Germany to defend your country. You became a pillar in the defence of Sarajevo, a man of courage people could trust," Sead Hasic, Caco's boyhood friend and brigade comrade, said in a eulogy.
"Some tried to accuse you but for most you were an example, especially to the poor," Hasic said of Caco, who was said to have given some of his booty to the poor under siege.

But Caco's men also kidnapped businessmen for ransom, killing some, stole cash, fuel, armoured cars and bulletproof vests at gunpoint from foreign aid workers and journalists, and pressganged civilians into front-line combat.
His disciples said the government would never have found enough men to defend the capital if Caco had not rounded up shirkers in the street and in raids on cafes and restaurants.
However, the Bosnian government feared the breakdown of law and order in Sarajevo would drive out Western benefactors and in October 1993 security forces pounced on Caco.

He and 100 of his followers were captured after days of house-by-house gunbattles that paralysed the city as the Serbs paused to watch, their media deriding the intra-Moslem carnage. Twenty-one people were killed, including a few bystanders.

Caco, 37, was shot dead a day later while trying to escape, the government said. But some army sources said he was executed in custody by the father of one of nine policemen murdered after being taken hostage by Caco.

"Some of his men may have committed brutalities but not Caco. His undoing was a power struggle between the army and (security) police," insisted Mehmed Alija Trbic, a former 10th Mountain Brigade soldier.
"His great service was mobilising men for war when the government failed to do the job."
Sarajevo's commercially bustling Old Town came to a standstill and women wept as Caco's funeral cortege surged through the cobbled warrens en route to the cemetery.
